plan.contextChunk: This figure builds a recursion tree in four labeled stages, (a), (b), and (c) running across the top and (d) occupying the lower two-thirds. Part (a) is just the term T(n), printed at the upper left. Part (b) replaces it with a root cn whose two edges descend to T(n/2) and T(n/2). Part (c) carries the expansion one step further: the root cn branches to cn/2 and cn/2, and each of those branches to two nodes reading T(n/4). Part (d) shows the fully expanded tree, with cn at the top, two cn/2 nodes on the next level, four cn/4 nodes below them, short dashed edges continuing downward, and a bottom row of the constant c repeated with an ellipsis through its middle; a horizontal brace under that row is labeled n. A double-headed vertical arrow at the far left spans the full height and is labeled "lg n". To the right of each drawn level a dotted arrow points across to that level's total, and all four of these read cn, with a vertical ellipsis standing in for the levels not drawn; a rule beneath the column carries "Total: cn lg n + cn". Stacking the level sums in a single right-hand column makes the equality of every level's cost the visible fact, so that height alone determines the sum. The staged expansion from (a) to (d) shows where the tree comes from before the costs are added.

interactionPlan.concept: A recursion tree for T(n)=2T(n/2)+cn has total cost cn on every internal level, lg n such levels, and cn total leaf cost, giving cn lg n + cn = Θ(n lg n).

interactions.label: Expand recurrence
interactions.teaches: Each expansion replaces an unresolved T(size) term with the local cost for that subproblem plus two smaller recursive calls, building the recursion tree level by level

interactions.label: Problem size n = 2^k
interactions.teaches: Doubling n adds one more recursion level, so the tree height grows as lg n while the number of leaves grows as n

demo_steps.title: Start with the recurrence
demo_steps.narration: The tree begins with one unresolved problem, T(n). The recurrence says solving it requires two half-size subproblems plus cn work at the current level.

demo_steps.title: Expand once
demo_steps.narration: Replacing T(n) by the recurrence creates a root cost cn and two unresolved children T(n/2). This is the first branching of the divide-and-conquer process.

demo_steps.title: Expand again
demo_steps.narration: Each T(n/2) becomes a cost cn/2 plus two calls on n/4. The second level has two nodes, but each costs half as much.

demo_steps.title: See the full tree
demo_steps.narration: The pattern continues until subproblems reach size 1, producing n leaves of cost c. The tree height is lg n.

demo_steps.title: Change n
demo_steps.narration: Move the slider: increasing k makes n=2^k larger, adds leaves, and extends the lg n height marker by one level each time. The per-level total remains cn, so the number of levels controls the asymptotic cost.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Although the tree doubles in width each level, each node's cost halves, so every internal level sums to cn and the lg n levels give Θ(n lg n).
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean black-and-white textbook style with italic serif math labels. Arrange stages (a), (b), and (c) across the top, and the full tree (d) below them. In the interactive version, the expansion button may emphasize or replace the active stage while keeping the same visual language. The full tree should show only the first few levels explicitly, then dashed continuation edges and ellipses to avoid clutter for large n. The slider value k represents n=2^k; update labels such as lg n, the brace label n, the number of displayed leaf markers, and the final total accordingly. When the level-cost overlay is on, lightly highlight one row at a time or all rows, and show dotted arrows to the right-hand column where every displayed level total reads cn, ending with 'Total: cn lg n + cn' beneath a short horizontal rule.

authoredContext: Figure 2.5 shows how we can solve recurrence (2.2). For convenience, we assume that n is an exact power of 2. Part (a) of the figure shows T .n/, which we expand in part (b) into an equivalent tree representing the recurrence. The cn term is the root (the cost incurred at the top level of recursion), and the two subtrees of the root are the two smaller recurrences T .n=2/. Part (c) shows this process carried one step further by expanding T .n=2/. The cost incurred at each of the two subnodes at the second level of recursion is cn=2. We continue expanding each node in the tree by breaking it into its constituent parts as determined by the recurrence, until the problem sizes get down to 1, each with a cost of c. Part (d) shows the resulting recursion tree. Next, we add the costs across each level of the tree. The top level has total cost cn, the next level down has total cost c.n=2/ C c.n=2/ D cn, the level after that has total cost c.n=4/Cc.n=4/Cc.n=4/Cc.n=4/ D cn, and so on. In general, the level i below the top has 2 i nodes, each contributing a cost of c.n=2i /, so that the ith level below the top has total cost 2 i c.n=2i / D cn. The bottom level has n nodes, each contributing a cost of c, for a total cost of cn. The total number of levels of the recursion tree in Figure 2.5 is lg n C 1, where n is the number of leaves, corresponding to the input size. An informal inductive argument justifies this claim. The base case occurs when n D 1, in which case the tree has only one level. Since lg 1 D 0, we have that lg n C 1 gives the correct number of levels. Now assume as an inductive hypothesis that the number of levels of a recursion tree with 2 i leaves is lg 2 i C 1 D i C 1 (since for any value of i, we have that lg 2 i D i). Because we are assuming that the input size is a power of 2, the next input size to consider is 2 iC1 . A tree with n D 2 iC1 leaves has one more level than a tree with 2 i leaves, and so the total number of levels is .i C 1/ C 1 D lg 2 iC1 C 1. To compute the total cost represented by the recurrence (2.2), we simply add up the costs of all the levels. The recursion tree has lg n C 1 levels, each costing cn, for a total cost of cn.lg n C 1/ D cn lg n C cn. Ignoring the low-order term and the constant c gives the desired result of ‚.n lg n/.

discrepancies: The default rendering adds pale yellow highlight boxes and horizontal row highlights around the full tree, whereas the source figure is entirely black-and-white with no shaded emphasis regions.
An extra recurrence label, "T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn", is drawn across the top panels; this text is not present in the source and visually interferes with panel (b).
The rightmost T(n/4) label in panel (c) is positioned beyond the viewbox edge and is likely clipped or too close to the boundary, unlike the source where all labels sit comfortably inside the figure.
The UI step narration says the figure is at the initial T(n) stage, but the displayed stage is the full tree with overlays enabled, so the default interactive state is internally inconsistent.
Several labels in the rendered screenshot are very small at inline size, especially in the upper panels and lower full-tree leaf row, reducing the readability compared with the source.

The full-tree leaf row is represented with many evenly spaced explicit c labels and a central ellipsis, which is acceptable conceptually but does not closely match the source's sparser leaf continuation layout.
evaluation.notes: The recurrence-tree structure and level-sum concept are largely correct and recognizable, but the default view adds non-source highlights and extra text, has a clipped top-panel label, and starts in a state inconsistent with the narration.

Remove the extra top-panel recurrence equation or move it into the UI narration/popup instead of placing it on the figure.
Reposition or rescale panel (c), especially the rightmost T(n/4) label, so no text is clipped at the viewbox edge.
Initialize with applyStep(0) or change the initial narration/step label so the visible stage and UI state agree.

demo_steps.narration: Move the slider: increasing k makes n=2^k larger, adds leaves, and extends the lg n height marker by one level each time. The per-level total remains cn, so the number of levels controls the asymptotic cost.

plan.keyInsight: Although the tree doubles in width each level, each node's cost halves, so every internal level sums to cn and the lg n levels give Θ(n lg n).
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean black-and-white textbook style with italic serif math labels. Arrange stages (a), (b), and (c) across the top, and the full tree (d) below them. In the interactive version, the expansion button may emphasize or replace the active stage while keeping the same visual language. The full tree should show only the first few levels explicitly, then dashed continuation edges and ellipses to avoid clutter for large n. The slider value k represents n=2^k; update labels such as lg n, the brace label n, the number of displayed leaf markers, and the final total accordingly. When the level-cost overlay is on, lightly highlight one row at a time or all rows, and show dotted arrows to the right-hand column where every displayed level total reads cn, ending with 'Total: cn lg n + cn' beneath a short horizontal rule.

discrepancies: the generated top mini-panel (c) is noticeably more compressed than the source, with the right-hand T(n/4) labels crowded together and close to the edge
the interactive problem-size slider changes the leaf labels and bottom n value but does not actually add visible recursion levels or lengthen the lg n height marker as the narration claims

the full-tree leaf row shows a different schematic distribution of c leaves and ellipsis than the source, with more evenly generated leaf positions rather than the source's grouped leaves under the drawn branches

evaluation.notes: The generated figure is clearly recognizable and captures the recurrence-tree structure, labels, dotted level-sum arrows, brace, height marker, and total formula well, but some labels are crowded and the size-slider interaction overstates changes that are not actually reflected in the tree geometry.
action_items: Increase the horizontal spacing in top panel (c), especially the rightmost T(n/4) pair, so the labels match the source spacing and remain comfortably readable.
Make the problem-size slider redraw the full tree consistently with k by adding or schematically indicating additional recursion levels and adjusting the lg n arrow length.
Tune the bottom leaf row to more closely match the source: grouped c leaves under the visible subtrees, a centered ellipsis, and fewer mechanically uniform leaf positions.
Keep optional focus boxes and gray overlays visually subtle or hidden by default so the initial state remains a closer drop-in replacement for the textbook figure.
